It sounds when the heel of the hand, the fingers, the thumb and the palm strike the outside wall, and different striking points and parts of the hand give different timbres. The bass is made by pressing the pot against the belly and releasing it, and by striking with the lower wrist; the treble by striking different points with the fingers. A beginner should first fix the distance between the mouth and the belly, then practise the different parts of the hand and striking points, using the same drum syllables as the mridangam.

Its name comes from the Sanskrit ghaṭa ('pot') and the related word kuṇḍa ('water jar'); in Tamil, ghaṭam refers specifically to the percussion instrument, while in Sanskrit it was a general term. In the Punjab the instrument has a variant, the gharha, part of the Punjabi folk tradition; similar instruments in Rajasthan are called madga and pani mataqa. The matka of Gujarat and Rajasthan was originally used to store water, make yoghurt or cook, and when used as an instrument it is called ghara, mostly in folk music. The main place of manufacture is Manamadurai in Tamil Nadu, and they are also made in Chennai and Bangalore.

The ghatam is a percussion instrument of the Indian subcontinent, especially South India. It is made from clay fired into a narrow-mouthed pot, often with brass or copper powder and a little iron powder mixed in, and the wall must be of even thickness; the pitch varies with the size of the pot and can be adjusted with plasticine or water. When played it rests on the lap with its mouth facing the belly, and the heel of the hand, the fingers, the thumb and the palm strike the outside wall while the distance between pot and belly changes the timbre; it suits fast rhythms. It is often played together with the mridangam in concert, and the Punjab and Rajasthan also have related folk variants.
